No megaproject designation for this project was found (see negative_searches). The 30-year tier is therefore unavailable to it on this record — it depends on a state designation nobody has shown exists.

That is one prong of a disjunctive test and omits the wage floor.

disclosed_economics.source: the Project Overview the City posted (developer-authored)

as_written.noise_investment: tens of millions in noise-dampening technology

correction.what_the_source_says: The two figures MUST NOT be added. The Project Overview states the schools' ">$2,800,000" is drawn "(from the total revenue)" — i.e. it is a component of the ">$3,000,000", not an addend. The disclosed aggregate is therefore "over $3,000,000" annually, roughly half what the corpus and the issue text carried.

auditor_basis.note: Because the CRA exempts only "the increase in assessed valuation resulting from improvements" and the assembly currently carries ZERO improvement value, the whole of a ~$1B build would be the exemptible increase. The land stays on the roll either way.

reconciliation.implied_millage_inversion: Ohio assesses real property at 35% of true value, so a $1B improvement is ~$350M of assessed value. For that to yield only the disclosed ">$3,000,000" a year across ALL taxing bodies implies an effective rate of about 8.6 mills — far below any plausible Ohio commercial effective rate. The disclosed figure therefore CANNOT represent unabated property tax on the improvement. It is consistent only with (a) a substantial abatement of the improvement value, plus (b) revenue that a CRA does not abate — municipal income tax on construction and operations payroll, and any negotiated school compensation.
reconciliation.corroborating_city_datum: [verified] The City's own share of the property tax is small: Resolution 2721-25 (considered 2025-10-21, FAILED 2-5) would have reduced "the City of Urbana's share of the General Fund (Inside) property tax collection from 1.8 mills to 1.5 mills." At 1.8 mills the City's own unabated take on $350M of assessed improvement would be ~$630,000/yr — well under the ">$3,000,000" attributed to "the City of Urbana," which reinforces that the disclosed figure is a jurisdiction-wide, mixed-source number rather than a municipal property-tax line.
reconciliation.school_consent_threshold: [verified as said] Urbana City Schools treasurer Mandy Hildebrand told the 2025-10-21 hearing that the statute allows up to a 75% abatement without going to the school board, that the board "has questions whenever a 100% abatement is asked for," that recent requests have been under 100%, and that revenue sharing becomes possible when total payroll exceeds $2 million. She was explicit that she spoke neither for nor against the designation.
reconciliation.unresolved: [open] The effective millage for the Urbana City School District tax district, and Urbana's municipal income-tax rate, are both needed to close this arithmetic. Neither the county auditor nor the Ohio Department of Taxation is reachable from this environment.

land_spend_reconciliation.city_statement: "the developer entered into agreements with the participating property owners for approximately $5,000,000" and, more specifically, "purchases of 47 acres ... for just over $2 million, and in November the developer purchased just over 80 acres ... for just over $3 million."
land_spend_reconciliation.finding: The City's "approximately $5,000,000" reconciles EXACTLY to the two Brand Investments deeds recorded before the notice was written — $5,354,377.50 — and its "47 acres"/"just over 80 acres" match the recorded 47.637 ac and 85.619 ac. The third conveyance (Organ Farms → Urbana Owner II, $3,398,150, recorded 2026-06-12) postdates the notice; all three total $8,752,527.50. This is a clean two-source corroboration of the land-assembly register AND it confirms the City treats the Urbana Owner I / Highland55 SPEs as "the developer."

counts.title: Procedural Due Process
counts.gist: Deprivation of a vested property/liberty interest in the data-center use without lawful process (notice, fair BZA hearing, consideration of evidence).

counts.title: Substantive Due Process
counts.gist: The moratorium, application denial, and appeal handling were arbitrary, capricious, and lacking any substantial relation to legitimate land-use regulation.

counts.title: Declaratory Judgment — Moratorium void (Charter § 2.12)
counts.gist: Charter § 2.12 bars enacting/amending/repealing any zoning or building resolution as an emergency; the moratorium is a de facto zoning amendment.

counts.title: Declaratory Judgment — Moratorium void (Charter § 2.11)
counts.gist: Res. 2727-26 is not necessary for public peace/health/welfare/safety and does not set forth the specific facts necessitating the emergency.

counts.title: Declaratory Judgment — Moratorium void (Ohio Const. Art. XVIII §3 + R.C. 731.30)
counts.gist: The emergency exceeds the City's home-rule authority and R.C. 731.30's emergency-ordinance requirements.

counts.title: Declaratory Judgment — Moratorium void (Charter §§ 2.10, 2.16 + Zoning Code Ch. 1113)
counts.gist: No newspaper publication 7 days before enactment, no Planning-Commission referral, no 10-day notice, and passed on one reading (three required for permanent legislation).

counts.title: Declaratory Judgment — Moratorium an unlawful impairment of vested rights
counts.gist: Filing the Feb-13-2026 site-plan application froze the zoning rules (Golf Vill. N. LLC v. City of Powell; Gibson v. Oberlin); the later moratorium cannot retroactively defeat the vested use.

counts.title: Declaratory Judgment — Site-plan denial violated Zoning Code Ch. 1110
counts.gist: The City denied the application as 'incomplete' by importing Chapter 1161 (major-subdivision) requirements and a traffic study that Chapter 1110 site-plan review does not require — ultra vires.

key_authority_cited: Golf Vill. N. LLC v. City of Powell, 826 F. App'x 426, 433 (6th Cir. 2020) — filing an application 'freezes' the applicable zoning rules
Gibson v. Oberlin, 171 Ohio St. 1, 5 (1960) — vesting on application for a zoning certificate
Snyder v. City of Bowling Green, 1996 Ohio App. LEXIS 5580 (6th Dist.) — insufficient emergency basis
relief_sought: Declarations that the Moratorium (Res. 2727-26) is void ab initio on five independent grounds (Charter §§ 2.10/2.11/2.12/2.16, Zoning Ch. 1113, Ohio Const. Art. XVIII §3, R.C. 731.30)
Declaration that the site-plan denial violated Zoning Ch. 1110 and that the Application was complete
Declaration of a vested right to the data-center use under the rules in effect at filing
Preliminary + permanent injunction (Fed. R. Civ. P. 65) barring enforcement of the Moratorium and the amended Zoning Code against the Property, and directing approval of the Application
Pre-/post-judgment interest; attorney's fees under 42 U.S.C. § 1988; costs

alleged_facts: The City encouraged Thor's investment from Dec-2024 and gave repeated assurances (¶¶41–47).
The Feb-20-2026 'incomplete' denial was pretextual — the cited Ch. 1161 items don't govern site-plan review (¶¶56–59).
The moratorium was a pretext to stop an already-authorized use; council members admitted no information would change their minds (¶¶65–66).
The BZA hearing was procedurally defective: no lawful notice, denied continuance, only 4 of 5 members present (four votes needed to sustain an appeal), evidence disregarded (¶¶76–85).
